text: Before we go further there's one term I have to explain or the rest will get stuck, and that's embedding. An embedding turns a piece of text into a string of numbers, and those numbers preserve what the text means. The remarkable part is that two pieces of text meaning similar things come out as numbers that sit close together. Which means you can ask, mathematically, which sentence is most like this one. Think of it as giving every sentence a coordinate, where sentences with similar meanings land near each other on the map. Every bit of retrieval in this memory system runs on that.

text: Okay, back to the base version of Mem zero. It runs in two phases. The first is the extraction phase. Its job is to go through a pile of conversation and pull out the things worth remembering. The paper calls what comes out a candidate fact. Notice how carefully that word is chosen. Candidate. Not something we have decided to keep.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: This phase takes input from two different sources, and the design there is clever. The first source is a summary of the long conversation history, generated on a schedule by a separate language model. The second source is the last few messages, word for word, uncompressed. Why two? Because the summary covers the distant past — compressed, but broad. The raw messages cover what just happened — uncompressed, so the detail survives. Feed both in and you've covered near and far.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound crisp and brisk, like you're planting a signpost.
text: That's extraction. Now comes the part of this design that is genuinely hard.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: The second phase is the update phase, and this is where it gets tricky. Once a candidate fact comes out, you can't just drop it into the database. Why not? Because it might duplicate a memory you already hold, which wastes space. Or it might contradict one, which is worse — now your database carries two facts that fight each other. So the system takes the embedding of that candidate fact, finds the most similar existing memories in the database, puts the new one alongside the old ones, and hands the whole set to a language model to judge.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: The way it makes that judgment is function calling. In short: you don't let the model answer freely. You hand it a fixed set of options, require it to pick exactly one, and require the answer in a structured format. The benefit is that the output can be handed straight to your code, with no parsing of a free-form paragraph. That matters a lot in engineering, because free text varies in ways you will never anticipate, and a fixed set of options does not.

text: So what are the options?

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: There are exactly four, and I'll take them one at a time. The first is add: this is new information, put it in. The second is update: the old memory still stands but needs correcting with the new information. Say the user used to tell you they love spicy food, and later mentions their stomach has been bad lately. That's an update. The third is delete: the new and the old contradict each other, and the old one is wrong, so remove it. And the fourth is no op, which means do nothing at all. That is the entire memory management system. Four moves. There is no fifth.

text: I want to stop here, because I think the most valuable insight in this paper is hiding in the last two moves. Everybody does add and update. Those are the intuitive ones. Delete and no op are not. Being willing to remove something you already recorded means the system admits it might have recorded it wrong. Being willing to decide this isn't worth remembering means it admits not all information has value. Without those two, your memory store just gets bigger and dirtier, and in the end it's no different from dumping the whole conversation in.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound steady and clear, laying out the background.
text: The graph version starts from a very reasonable observation: memories have relationships between them, and a list cannot store a relationship. Here's an example. Say your memory store holds two facts. One, Alice lives in San Francisco. Two, San Francisco is in northern California. Now I ask you, where in California does Alice live? With a list you have to pull both of those out separately and then join them up yourself. But if you had stored it as a web from the beginning, there was already a line running between those two facts. You just follow it.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: So the graph version stores memory as a graph instead. That graph has three parts. First, nodes, which stand for entities — a person named Alice, or a place called San Francisco. Second, edges, which stand for the relationships between entities, like lives in. Third, labels, which say what kind of thing an entity is. Alice is labelled a person, San Francisco is labelled a city. On top of that, every node also carries its own embedding and the time it was created.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: String those three together and you get what the paper keeps calling a triplet. The format is source node, relationship, target node. Alice, lives in, San Francisco — that's one triplet. You can picture the whole memory web as an enormous pile of those stacked on top of each other. The advantage of this structure is that it is naturally suited to questions you can only answer by chaining several steps together.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: The graph version's extraction phase also splits into two steps, each with its own language model. Step one is entity extraction: pull every entity out of the conversation and tag what kind of thing it is. If the conversation is about a trip, you might get an origin, a destination, and a departure date, labelled place, place, and date. Step two is relationship generation: go back over those entities and work out how they relate. Origin to destination is a travelling from and to relationship. Departure date to destination is a when are you going relationship.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound crisp and brisk, like you're planting a signpost.
text: Once you have entities and relationships, you are facing the update problem all over again.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: The update logic is similar to the base version, but there is more to handle. When a new triplet arrives, the system takes the embeddings of the source and target nodes and searches the graph for similar existing nodes. Then two modules take over. The first is conflict detection, which finds where the new information fights with the old. The second is the update resolver, which decides what to do about it. The outcome might be adding both nodes, adding only one, or adding neither and simply updating what is already in the graph.

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound crisp and brisk, like you're planting a signpost.
text: That covers putting things in. How do you get them back out?

style: Speak in a neutral American accent, like the host of a tech podcast. Sound patient and precise, like you're explaining how something works.
text: For retrieval the graph version gives you two routes. The first is entity centric. You analyse which entities appear in the question, then pull the related nodes out of the graph along with the relationships between them, and assemble a small subgraph. That subgraph is the background you need to answer. The second route is semantic triplet. You turn the whole question into a single vector, compare it against the vectors of every triplet in the graph, and take the closest few. The first route runs on structure, the second on meaning. Two completely different ways of thinking about the same problem.

text: On implementation, the authors use Neo4j as the graph database, which is the mainstream choice today. text: To compare two systems you need a shared exam, and in research that exam is called a benchmark. It's the same idea as a standardized test: everyone sits the same paper, so the scores can be put side by side. Which means how good the benchmark is decides how much you can trust the paper's conclusion. Keep that in mind. It becomes important later.

text: The exam they picked is called LOCOMO, built specifically to evaluate long-term memory in conversational systems. Here's the scale of it. Ten conversations in total. Each one averages about six hundred messages, which works out to roughly twenty-six thousand tokens in the units a model actually sees. And each conversation comes with around two hundred questions, every one with a reference answer. Picture two people talking for a very long time, and then someone writing an exam out of the transcript.

text: The questions come in four categories, and these four keep coming back, so one sentence each. The first is single hop: the answer sits in one message, and once you find that message you're done. The second is multi hop: you have to chain several messages together, like the Alice and San Francisco example from earlier. The third is temporal, which tests order in time — did he move before or after he changed jobs? The fourth is open domain, where the question is looser and there's no fixed scope.

text: They use three metrics. The first two are traditional. One is the F1 score, which looks at two things at once: of what the model said, how much was right, and of everything it should have said, how much did it catch. Both have to be good for the score to be good. The second is BLEU, which was built for machine translation, and measures how much the model's output overlaps with the reference answer word for word. The shared problem with both is that they compare the words.

You take another language model, have it read the model's answer next to the reference answer, and decide whether the two mean the same thing. That is much closer to how a person would judge it, which is why most of the later charts use it.

Get one relationship wrong and the whole path breaks, and multi hop is exactly the category that depends most on paths staying intact. Put another way: the ceiling of a graph structure is very high, but its floor is very low, and the floor is set by extraction quality.

I think that framing matters much more than who won. When you're choosing a memory approach, the real question isn't which score is higher. What LOCOMO does is generate conversations and attach comprehension questions, which is still, at bottom, a reading test. But long-term memory in real life is tested months later, in a situation nobody anticipated, when the system has to surface the right thing on its own. text: If you're about to build a memory system yourself, I'd suggest answering two questions before you pick any technology. Question one: in your use case, does old information expire? If it does, then your delete and update logic matters more than your retrieval accuracy. Question two: do your questions require chaining relationships together? If they don't, a graph structure will probably hand you complexity without handing you accuracy, and this paper's own numbers are the best evidence of that.
